newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean students riot, demand president step down.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean students riot, demand president step down.

text.p: More than 10,000 South Korean students went on the rampage in Seoul on Saturday, infuriated by the refusal of President Kim Young-sam to reveal his election campaign spending.
Chanting "Bring down Kim Young-sam" and "Reveal the Election Funds", they hurled Molotov cocktails at riot police in skirmishes across wide areas of the capital.
One young rioter was badly hurt after his shirt was set ablaze in by far the worst student violence since an uprising at Seoul's Yonsei University last August.
Another was in critical condition after collapsing from a heart attack during an earlier round of protests on Friday, Yonhap Television News reported.

Some of the fiercest clashes occurred outside the Shilla Hotel. Tourist buses and taxis ran a gauntlet of rock-throwing protesters to get in and out of the luxury establishment, and occasionally had to ferry terrified passengers at high speed across sheets of fire set by petrol bombs.
A televised address by President Kim on Friday ignited the student movement, which had been on the defensive since a massive police assault ended the seven-day rebellion at Yonsei.
Kim rebuffed opposition demands to reveal exactly how much his 1992 election cost, admitting only to having spent "enormous sums". He called for election reform.
Students were emboldened by the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, which has declared an all-out battle against Kim to uncover the truth.
The National Congress maintains that Kim's campaign was partly bankrolled by the scandal-ridden Hanbo Group and his disgraced predecessor, Roh Tae-woo, and far exceeded the legal spending limit.
The militant Hanchongryon organisation orchestrated Saturday's clashes. It has been branded by the government as a threat to public security because of its alleged links to rival North Korea.
Groups of militant students cruised Seoul's subway system, emerging periodically to confront police at station entrances.

Dressed in baseball caps and jeans, long snakes of students were guided through the subway by militant leaders in a game of cat-and-mouse with squadrons of riot police, who were backed on the streets by armoured tear-gas launchers.
Witnesses said some of the students were were chased down and bludgeoned by police officers.

The government seemed to have quashed the student movement after 151 Hanchongryon leaders were jailed following the Yonsei violence. But the students are now riding a surge of popular anger against the president.
Newspaper polls on Saturday showed most Koreans were angered by Kim's refusal to come clean on his finances. Kim had insisted it was impossible to account for his spending.

The Joong-ang Ilbo newspaper said 80.6 percent of South Koreans were disgruntled by the president's speech, while the Hankook Ilbo said 78.1 percent of Koreans thought the president's apology did not go far enough.
Kim apologised in general terms for spending abuses that he said were the legacy of a corrupt political system.
